>From this thread I was able to determine the possible offspring genotypes for parents with phase ABxAA (using your example for AAxAB above).

        ABxAB   ABxBA   BAxAB   BAxBA    <- parents' phase

Just want to make sure that it is OK if the possible genotypes are flipped (BC versus CB). This is true for all the numeric codes from the AB row so I just want to clarify.
Thanks for the help!

I'm not sure what you mean by "am I right here?"

Regarding effect plots: both effectplot() and plotPXG() will attempt to
infer the full genotypes AC,AD,BC,BD in a 4-way cross and will plot the
phenotypes or phenotype averages against those. So even if a given SNP
is not able to distinguish all four genotypes, R/qtl uses surrounding
markers to infer the full information.

karl

messages.body_plain:
If you use n.perm=1 then it doesn't matter what batchsize is, you'll just get a single permutation replicate.
batchsize takes the n.perm permutations and breaks them into groups and analyses them together, but if batchsize > n.perm then it's the same as if batchsize=n.perm.

Look at the permutation output to make sure they look reasonable; plot histograms.

calc.penalties calculates the main, heavy, and light penalties, and stepwise() makes use of them.

karl

> > My questions are:

> > Did I over fit the MQM model with 22 ramaining cofactor, given the population that I have (178 recombinant inbred lines, 175 of which were typed)?
> No in theory not. The MQM routine can handle upto (n individuals - 10) = ~ 165 cofactors, with 155 you're below this theorectical threshold,
> However,I would not go that high. My advice is to take ~ 100 cofactors into the model selection phase to prevent overfitting
>
> > For LOD profile around Q1 (overall MQM LOD profile, Fig. 2), did the MQM model used all Q2-Q22 as covariates and how did it do that given the population only consists of 175 typed RILs?
>
> Yes, this is exactly what the MQM routine does. MQM compensates for all other cofactors, in your case you loose 21 out of
> 174 degrees of freedom in the statistical test, this is perfectly reasonable
> > How can there be so many more QTLs detected by MQM method whilst only three were detected from both scanone() abd scantwo()? Are the MQM results reliable?
> scanone does not compensate for the cofactors used in the model, this is why MQM has higher statistical power to detect effects.
> However you should adjust the threshold using permutations where you include the same number of initial cofactors, my guess is

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Interpretation of stepwiseQTL
messages.body_plain:
The output of stepwiseqtl() is a qtl object. You can use it in fitqtl() to fit the specific model and get the drop-one-QTL-at-a-time table which would give you information about the strength of evidence of the individual QTL. The output of stepwiseqtl() should also include a formula which indicates which QTL are involved in interactions. You would want to provide that formula to fitqtl() so that you're consider the selected model and not the strictly additive one.

The system for selecting multiple-QTL models including interactions is described in Chapter 9 of the R/qtl book; also see Manichaikul et al (2009), https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.108.094565 The way in which the thresholds are turned into penalties is somewhat complicated.

The "one" column in the scantwoperm output is for the single-QTL model; it should correspond to what you get if you did a permutation test with scanone().

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Interpretation of stepwiseQTL
messages.body_plain:
If there are no interactions to be considered, then you can use the scanone permutation threshold to gauge the value of those individual QTL's LOD scores.

Interactions are more complicated if you're using the "light" and "heavy" interaction penalties. But you're pretty much comparing them to one or the other of those.

For QTL that are involved in an interaction, dropping the QTL involves dropping the interaction as well, so you'd look at the main-effect penalty plus a light or heavy interaction penalty.

What you want to think about are the different multiple-QTL models and try to derive the penalized LOD scores for them, with preference to the model with largest penalized LOD score.

Note that if you adjust the stringency of the penalties, the relative value of different models will change.

karl
